p.src: Now the fiend carried Bajie into the cave and said, “Brother, I have brought one of them back.” The elder demon said delightedly, “Bring him here and let me see.” The second demon said, “Here he is, is he not?” The elder demon said, “Brother, you have caught the wrong one. This monk is of no use.” Bajie seized on those words and said, “Great King, if this monk is of no use, then let him go. It is hardly proper to detain him.” The second demon said, “Brother, do not release him. Though he is useless, he is one of the Tang Monk’s company and is called Zhu Bajie. For now, soak him in the clear-water pool at the back until his hairy coat comes off, then salt and cure him, dry him in the sun, and save him as a relish for wine on a cloudy day.” Hearing this, Bajie said, “What rotten luck! I have fallen in with a demon who deals in cured meat.” The lesser demons carried Bajie inside and threw him into the water; of this no more for now.

p.src: Meanwhile, Tripitaka sat before the slope. His ears burned, his eyes twitched, and he felt uneasy. He called out, “Wukong, why has Wuneng been gone so long on this patrol of the mountain without returning?” The Pilgrim said, “Master, you still do not understand what is in his mind.” Tripitaka asked, “What is in his mind?” The Pilgrim replied, “Master, if there were monsters on this mountain, he would scarcely dare take half a step. He would certainly make a great show of alarm and run back to report to me. I expect there were no monsters and the road was peaceful, so he simply went straight on.” Tripitaka said, “If he truly has gone on ahead, where are we to meet him? This is a vast and empty wilderness, nothing like the inns, markets, and towns.” The Pilgrim said, “Do not worry, Master. Please mount the horse for now. That idiot is rather lazy, so he is certain to be walking slowly. Urge the horse on a little, and we shall surely catch him; then we can all travel together.” So the Tang Monk mounted his horse, Friar Sand shouldered the luggage, and the Pilgrim led the way up the mountain.

p.src: Meanwhile, the elder demon again summoned the second demon and said, “Brother, since you have captured Bajie, the Tang Monk must certainly be nearby. Go patrol the mountain once more, and be sure not to let him slip past.” The second demon replied, “I shall go at once, at once.” And there he was, hurriedly mustering fifty lesser demons to patrol the mountain. As they went, he suddenly saw auspicious clouds drifting faintly and blessed vapors curling in the air. The second demon said, “The Tang Monk is coming.” The demons asked, “Where is the Tang Monk?” The second demon said, “Auspicious clouds shine above the heads of good men, while black vapors surge skyward above the wicked. That Tang Monk is the Elder Golden Cicada descended to the mortal world, a good man who has cultivated himself through ten lifetimes; that is why these auspicious clouds drift above him.” None of the other demons could see them. The second demon pointed with his hand and said, “Is that not he?” At that very moment, Tripitaka shuddered on his horse; when the demon pointed again, he shuddered once more. The demon pointed three times in succession, and Tripitaka shuddered three times in succession. Deeply uneasy, he said, “Disciples, why am I shuddering so?” Friar Sand said, “Perhaps the shuddering means that an illness from indigestion has broken out.” The Pilgrim said, “Nonsense. Master is traveling through these steep and lonely mountains, so he must have taken fright from being overly wary. Do not be afraid, do not be afraid. Let old Monkey wield his staff along the road and settle your nerves.”

p.src: Our splendid Pilgrim readied his staff and performed several routines before the horse—three strokes above and four below, five to the left and six to the right—all in accordance with the Six Secret Teachings and the Three Strategies, as he brought his magic powers into play. Watching him from horseback, the elder saw a display truly rare beneath heaven and unequalled in all the world. He cleared a path and went straight ahead, very nearly frightening the monster senseless. Watching from the mountaintop, the monster was scared out of his wits and suddenly cried aloud, “For years I have heard tell of Sun the Pilgrim; only today do I know that the stories were no idle rumor, but entirely true.” The demons came forward and said, “Great King, why do you raise another’s morale and diminish your own might? Whom are you praising?” The second demon said, “Sun the Pilgrim possesses immense magic powers. We shall not succeed in eating the Tang Monk.” The demons said, “Great King, if you lack the means, let some of us report to the Great Great King. Have him muster every soldier in our cave and draw them up in battle formation. If we join forces and unite our hearts, how could he possibly escape?” The second demon said, “You have not seen that iron staff of his. It has the valor to withstand ten thousand men. There are no more than four or five hundred soldiers in our cave. How could they withstand a single blow from it?” The demons said, “If that is so, we cannot eat the Tang Monk, and did we not capture Zhu Bajie for nothing? Let us send him back now.” The second demon said, “Capturing him was not a mistake, but neither should we lightly send him back. We shall eat the Tang Monk eventually; it simply cannot be done just now.” The demons asked, “Does that mean we must wait several more years?” The second demon replied, “There is no need to wait for years. As I see it, the Tang Monk can only be taken through gentle schemes, not by violent force. If we try to seize him by relying on brute strength, we shall not even get a taste of him. We can only move him through kindness, beguiling him until his heart accords with mine. Then, from within that seeming kindness, I can devise a stratagem to take him.” The demons asked, “Great King, if you have settled on a plan to capture him, will you have need of us?” The second demon said, “All of you return to your own strongholds, and none of you is to tell the Great King; if he is roused, word will surely leak out and my plan will be ruined. I have a magical transformation of my own with which I can capture him.” The demons dispersed.

p.src: Now Tripitaka, heartened by the presence of the Great Sage Sun and Sha Monk, journeyed cheerfully onward. As they went, they suddenly heard a cry: “Master, save me!” Hearing it, Tripitaka said, “Mercy! Mercy! There are no villages or dwellings anywhere in these wild mountains. Who can be calling? Someone must have been struck down by a tiger, leopard, wolf, or other beast.” The elder turned his fine horse around and called, “Who is it that is in distress? Come out.” The monster crawled out of the grass and, before the elder’s horse, repeatedly knocked his head upon the ground. From horseback Tripitaka saw that he was a Daoist and an elderly man besides, and felt deeply embarrassed. He hurriedly dismounted, helped him up, and said, “Please rise, please rise.” The monster cried, “It hurts! It hurts! It hurts!” When Tripitaka released his hand and looked, he saw blood flowing from the man’s foot. Tripitaka asked in alarm, “Sir, where have you come from? How did you injure your honored foot?” With clever words and feigned sincerity, the monster replied, “Master, west of this mountain stands a secluded Daoist temple. I am a priest of that temple.” Tripitaka said, “Why are you wandering here instead of tending the incense and studying the scriptures and rites in your own temple?” The demon said, “The day before yesterday, a patron’s household south of the mountain invited our clergy to perform rites for averting astral calamities and bestowing blessings. My disciple and I left late and traveled together along the road. When we reached a remote part of the road, a brilliantly striped tiger suddenly appeared and carried off my disciple in its jaws. Trembling with fear, I had nowhere to flee. I fell upon a rocky slope, injured my leg and foot, and lost the way home. Today, by a great providence of Heaven, I have met you, Master. I beg you to show great compassion and save my life. If I can reach my temple, I shall pledge my very person and life to repay your profound kindness.” Tripitaka took these words for truth and said, “Sir, you and I alike possess but one life. I am a Buddhist monk and you a Daoist; though our robes and caps differ, the principle of spiritual cultivation is the same. If I did not save you, I would be unworthy of the religious life. I shall save you, certainly, but you cannot walk.” The monster said, “I cannot even stand. How could I walk?”

p.src: Tripitaka said, “Very well, very well. I can still walk, so I shall let you ride my horse for a while. When we reach your temple, you may return it to me.” The monster replied, “Master, I am deeply grateful for your kindness, but my leg and hip were injured in the fall, so I cannot ride.” “That is true,” said Tripitaka. He called to Sha Monk, “Strap the luggage onto my horse and carry him for a while.” Sha Monk said, “I will carry him.” The monster hastily turned and cast him a sidelong glance, saying, “Master, that fierce tiger frightened me badly. The sight of this master’s ill-omened dark face frightens me still more. I dare not let him carry me.” Tripitaka called, “Wukong, you carry him.” The Pilgrim answered eagerly, “I will, I will.” The demon settled on the Pilgrim and docilely allowed himself to be carried, saying nothing more. Sha Monk laughed and said, “What a blind old Daoist! He will not let me carry him, but insists on being carried by him. Once our master is out of sight, he will smash you upon a three-pointed rock and break every sinew in your body.”

p.src: Hearing this, the Pilgrim laughed to himself and thought, “You wretched demon, how dare you come and provoke me? You should ask how many years old old Sun is! Such ghostly lies might deceive the Tang Monk, but do you think they can deceive me too? I know you are a monster of this mountain, and I suppose you mean to eat my master. But my master is no ordinary man. Is he for the likes of you to eat? If you mean to eat him, you must give old Sun more than half.” Hearing the Pilgrim muttering, the demon said, “Master, I am the descendant of a respectable family and became a Daoist priest. Today I had the misfortune to suffer an attack by a tiger. I am no monster.” The Pilgrim said, “If you fear tigers and wolves, why do you not recite the Scripture of the Northern Dipper?” Tripitaka was just mounting his horse. When he heard this, he scolded, “You impudent monkey! ‘Saving one life is better than building a seven-storied pagoda.’ Just carry him, and say no more about the Scripture of the Northern Dipper or the Scripture of the Southern Dipper.” Hearing this, the Pilgrim thought, “This fellow is in luck. My master is kindhearted and charitable, though outwardly pleasant and inwardly prickly. If I refuse to carry you, he will blame me. Carry you I shall, but I must make one thing clear: if you need to relieve yourself, tell me first. If you let it run down my back, the stench will be unbearable, my clothes will be soiled, and there will be no one to wash them.” The monster said, “At my advanced age, would I not understand what you mean?” Only then did the Pilgrim pull him up, take him upon his back, and head west along the main road with the elder and Sha Monk. Wherever the mountain path was rough and uneven, the Pilgrim walked carefully and slowly, allowing the Tang Monk to go ahead.

p.src: They had gone no more than three or five li when his master and Sha Monk descended into a mountain hollow and vanished from the Pilgrim’s sight. He grumbled inwardly, “Master is so old, yet still understands nothing. On such a long journey, even when empty-handed one finds one’s hands a burden and wishes they could be cast away, yet he makes me carry this monster besides. Even if he were not a monster but a good man, at his age he has lived long enough to die. I should smash him to death. Why carry him?” Just as the Great Sage was considering how to dash him down, the monster perceived his intent; moreover, he knew the art of commanding mountains. He employed a spell for moving mountains and overturning seas, formed a hand seal and recited an incantation upon the Pilgrim’s back, then summoned Mount Sumeru into the air to crash down upon the Pilgrim’s head. Startled, the Great Sage tilted his head, and the mountain came to rest upon his left shoulder and arm. He laughed, “My child, what weight-increasing magic are you using to press upon old Sun? This does not frighten me, though a balanced load is easy to carry while an unbalanced one is hard to endure.” The demon said, “One mountain cannot hold him down.” He recited another spell and summoned Mount Emei into the air to press down on him. The Pilgrim tilted his head the other way, and it came to rest upon his right shoulder and arm. See how he carried the two great mountains and sped like a shooting star to catch up with his master. At this sight the demon chief broke into a sweat all over and cried, “So he can carry mountains!” Steeling himself once more, he recited the incantation and summoned Mount Tai into the air, bringing it straight down upon the Pilgrim’s head. The Great Sage’s strength failed and his sinews went numb. Struck by the demon’s method of bringing Mount Tai down upon his crown, he was crushed until his three corpse-spirits shrieked and blood spurted from all seven apertures.

p.src: When the elder demon heard this, he was delighted and said, “Bring him here and let me see.” The second demon said, “Is this not the one?” The elder demon said, “Brother, you have brought the wrong one again.” The second demon said, “You told me to capture Tripitaka.” The elder demon said, “Yes, this is indeed Tripitaka, but you have not yet captured that formidable Sun Wukong. We must capture him before we can safely eat Tripitaka. Until he is caught, you must on no account touch any of his companions. That Monkey King has vast supernatural powers and countless transformations. If we eat his master, do you think he will accept it quietly? Once he comes raising havoc at our gate, we shall never know another peaceful day.” The second demon laughed. “Brother, you think far too highly of him. To hear you praise him, one would think his like was rare in Heaven and nowhere to be found on earth. From what I have seen, he is nothing more than that and has no great abilities.” The elder demon asked, “Have you captured him?” The second demon replied, “I sent three great mountains to pin him beneath them, and he cannot move an inch. That is why I was able to bring Tripitaka and Sha Monk here, together with the horse and luggage.” Hearing this, the elder demon was overjoyed. “What splendid fortune! What splendid fortune! Once that rogue is trapped, Tripitaka truly becomes meat for our mouths.” He called to the lesser demons, “Quickly prepare wine. I shall first offer your Second King a cup in honor of his achievement.” The second demon said, “Brother, let us put off the wine for now. Tell the underlings to fish Zhu Bajie out of the water and hang him up.” They therefore hung Bajie in the eastern gallery, Sha Monk on the western side, and Tripitaka in the middle; the white horse was led to the manger, and the luggage was taken inside.

p.src: His cries soon startled the mountain gods, the local earth deities, and the Guardians of the Five Directions. Convening them, the Golden-Headed Guardian asked, “Whose mountain is this?” The earth deities replied, “It is ours.” “And who is pinned beneath your mountain?” The earth deities replied, “We do not know who it is.” The Guardian said, “So you truly do not know. The one pinned there is Sun Wukong the Pilgrim, the Great Sage Equal to Heaven who caused havoc in the Celestial Palace five hundred years ago. He has now embraced the true faith and become Tripitaka’s disciple. How could you lend your mountains to demons to crush him? You are as good as dead! If he should free himself one day, do you think he will spare you? Even if he deals leniently with us, the earth deities will be sentenced to stand at a post, the mountain gods will be sent into exile, and we too shall be charged with grave dereliction.” Only then did the mountain gods and earth deities become frightened. “We truly did not know! We did not know! We merely heard the demon recite his mountain-dispatching spell, so we moved the mountains here. How could we have known it was the Great Sage Sun?” The Guardian said, “Do not be afraid for the moment. The law states, ‘Those who act in ignorance shall not be convicted.’ I shall devise a plan with you to release him without letting him raise his staff against us.” An earth deity said, “That would be utterly unreasonable. Why would he beat us after we released him?” The Guardian said, “You do not understand. He possesses an As-You-Will Gold-Banded Staff of tremendous power: anyone struck squarely by it dies, and anyone merely caught by its sweep is injured. A light knock from it snaps the sinews, and the merest brush strips away the skin.”

p.src: Terrified, the earth deities and mountain gods conferred with the Guardians of the Five Directions, then came outside the three mountains and called, “Great Sage, the mountain gods, earth deities, and Guardians of the Five Directions have come to see you.” Our fine Pilgrim, though the tiger had grown lean, had lost none of his proud heart. Wukong sprang up, shook off the dirt, straightened his robe, pulled the staff from behind his ear, and called to the mountain gods and earth deities, “All of you, stick out your shins. Let Old Sun give each of you two blows first, to relieve my vexation.” The gods were greatly alarmed. “The Great Sage just promised to pardon our offense. Why have you changed your word the moment you came out and now wish to beat us?” Wukong said, “Fine earth deities and mountain gods you are! You were not afraid of Old Sun, yet you feared those monsters?” An earth deity replied, “That demon possesses vast supernatural powers and mighty magic. By reciting true words and spells, he summons us to his cave and makes us take turns serving there, one of us on duty each day.”

p.src: When Wukong heard the words “on duty,” even he was startled. He raised his face to Heaven and cried aloud, “O Heaven! O Heaven! Ever since chaos first divided, Heaven opened, and earth was formed, and the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit gave me birth, I too have traveled far and wide in search of enlightened masters and was taught the secret of immortality. Think of how I could transform with the wind, subdue tigers and dragons, cause havoc in the Celestial Palace, and earn the title Great Sage—yet never did I tyrannically command the mountain gods and earth deities. Having given birth to Old Sun, why did you give birth to such creatures as these?”

p.src: While the Great Sage was lamenting, he saw a blaze of rosy light approaching through the hollow in the mountain. Pilgrim said, “Mountain God and Local Deity, since you serve in this cave, what is that thing giving off light?” The Local Deity replied, “That is the light from the fiends’ treasures. I expect some demons are bringing them to subdue you.” Pilgrim said, “Now this should be amusing. Let me ask you: who in this cave is on friendly terms with him?” The Local Deity replied, “He loves compounding elixirs and refining medicines, and is fond of Daoist adepts of the Complete Reality school.” Pilgrim said, “No wonder he changed into an old Daoist priest and tricked my master away. In that case, remember the beating you have had and go back now. Let old Monkey capture them himself.” All the deities soared into the air and dispersed.

p.src: Before long, the two little demons arrived. Pilgrim stretched out his gold-banded staff. The demons, taken unawares, caught their feet on it and fell sprawling with a thump. Scrambling up and only then seeing Pilgrim, they cried, “What a rogue! What a rogue! If our king did not respect you religious men, we would settle accounts with you.” Pilgrim smiled apologetically and said, “What accounts are there to settle? When one Daoist meets another, both belong to the same family.” The demon said, “Why were you lying here and tripping me up?” Pilgrim replied, “When a young Daoist acolyte meets an old priest like me, he must take a tumble as a greeting gift.” The demon said, “Our king asks only a few ounces of silver as a greeting gift. How can a tumble serve as one? Your district must have customs of its own; you are certainly no Daoist from these parts.” Pilgrim said, “Indeed I am not. I come from Mount Penglai.” The demon said, “Mount Penglai is an island realm of immortals.” Pilgrim replied, “If I am not an immortal, then who is?” The demons’ anger at once turned to delight. Stepping forward, they said, “Venerable immortal, venerable immortal! With our mortal eyes and fleshly bodies, we failed to recognize you and spoke offensively. Forgive us, forgive us.” Pilgrim said, “I do not blame you. As the saying goes, ‘An immortal’s body does not tread the mortal earth.’ How could you have known? I have come to your mountain today to guide one worthy person to immortality and attainment of the Way. Which of you is willing to come with me?” Sharp-witted Ghost said, “Master, I will go with you.” Clever Worm said, “Master, I will go with you.”

p.src: Though Pilgrim knew perfectly well, he deliberately asked, “Where have you two come from?” The demons replied, “From Lotus Flower Cave.” “And where are you going?” The demons replied, “Our king ordered us to capture Sun the Pilgrim.” Pilgrim asked, “Capture whom?” The demons repeated, “Sun the Pilgrim.” Sun the Pilgrim asked, “Do you mean the Sun the Pilgrim who is accompanying the Tang Monk in search of the scriptures?” The demons said, “The very one, the very one. Do you know him too?” Pilgrim said, “That monkey is rather insolent. I know him, and I bear him something of a grudge myself. I will help you capture him, and so lend you a hand.” The demons said, “Master, we need no help from you. Our second king has considerable magic. He sent three great mountains to pin the fellow beneath them, so that he cannot move an inch, and ordered the two of us to bring these treasures and put him away in them.” Pilgrim asked, “What treasures are they?” Sharp-witted Ghost said, “Mine is the red gourd, and his is the pure jade vase.” Pilgrim asked, “How do you put him inside?” The little demon replied, “We turn the treasure upside down, with its base toward heaven and its mouth toward the earth, then call his name. If he answers, he is drawn inside; then we paste on a talisman reading, ‘By the Supreme Lord Lao’s decree, swiftly obey the law,’ and in an hour and three quarters he will dissolve into pus.” Hearing this, Pilgrim was secretly alarmed. “Formidable, formidable!” he thought. “The Duty God of the Day warned me that they had five treasures; here are two of them. I wonder what the other three things may be?” Pilgrim smiled and said, “You two, lend me your treasures for a look.” Knowing nothing of his scheme, the little demons took the two treasures from their sleeves and presented them to Pilgrim with both hands. At the sight of them, Pilgrim rejoiced inwardly. “Fine things, fine things! If I flick up my tail and leap away with a whoosh, I can simply count them as gifts to old Monkey.” But then he thought, “No, no. I could certainly snatch them, but it would sully old Monkey’s good name. That would be outright robbery in broad daylight.” He handed them back, saying, “But you have not yet seen my treasure.” The demons asked, “What treasure do you have, Master? Lend it to us mortals for a look, that it may ward off misfortune.”

p.src: Our fine Pilgrim reached down, plucked a hair from his tail, rolled it between his fingers, and cried, “Change!” It instantly became a great purple-gold-and-red gourd, one foot seven inches long. Taking it from his waist, he said, “Would you like to see my gourd?” Clever Worm took it in his hands, examined it, and said, “Master, your gourd is large, well-shaped, and handsome, but it is useless.” Pilgrim asked, “How is it useless?” The demon replied, “Each of our two treasures can hold a thousand people.” Pilgrim said, “What is remarkable about yours merely holding people? This gourd of mine can hold even heaven itself.” The demon asked, “It can actually hold heaven?” Pilgrim replied, “It truly can hold heaven.” The demon said, “We fear that is a lie. Put heaven inside it for us to see, and then we shall believe you; otherwise, we will never believe you.” Pilgrim said, “If heaven provokes me, I usually put it away seven or eight times in a month. If it does not provoke me, I may go half a year without putting it away even once.” Clever Worm said, “Brother, let us trade our treasure for his heaven-holding one.” Sharp-witted Ghost replied, “Why would he exchange a heaven-holding treasure for our people-holding one?” Clever Worm said, “If he will not agree, we can throw in the pure vase as well.” Pilgrim rejoiced inwardly. “A gourd for a gourd, with the pure vase thrown in: two treasures for one. What a splendid bargain!” He immediately stepped forward, caught hold of Clever Worm, and asked, “Will you make the exchange if it holds heaven?” The demon replied, “If it really holds heaven, we shall trade. If we do not, I am your son.” Pilgrim said, “Very well, very well. I shall put heaven inside it for you to see.”

p.src: That day the Wandering Spirit went straight through the Southern Gate of Heaven to the foot of the Hall of Miraculous Mist, where he reported to the Jade Emperor and related all that had happened. The Jade Emperor said, “That impudent monkey speaks with no sense of propriety. Previously, Guanyin came and asked that he be released to protect the Tang Monk, and We also dispatched the Five Directional Guardians and the Four Duty Gods to watch over him in turn. And now he wants to borrow the sky to put it into a vessel. Can the sky possibly be contained?” No sooner had he said that it could not than Prince Nezha the Third stepped out from among the assembled ranks and memorialized, “Your Majesty, the sky can indeed be contained.” The Jade Emperor asked, “How can the sky be contained?” Nezha replied, “When Chaos was first divided, the light and pure became Heaven, while the heavy and turbid became Earth. The sky is a mass of pure ether supporting the jasper halls and palaces of Heaven; strictly speaking, it truly is difficult to contain. Yet Sun the Novice is escorting the Tang Monk westward to fetch the scriptures, a blessed destiny as lofty as Mount Tai and a store of merit as deep as the sea. Today we ought to help him succeed.” The Jade Emperor asked, “How do you propose to help him?” Nezha replied, “Issue a decree permitting me to go to the Northern Gate of Heaven and borrow the Black Carved Banner from Zhenwu. I shall unfurl it above the Southern Gate of Heaven and shut away the sun, moon, and stars. Then no one will be able to see the person opposite him or distinguish white from black. We can deceive the monsters by claiming that the sky has been put inside, and thus help the Novice succeed.” On hearing this, the Jade Emperor said, “Let it be as you have proposed.” Receiving the decree, the prince went to the Northern Gate of Heaven, met Zhenwu, and explained the whole affair. The Patriarch at once handed the banner to the prince.

p.src: The Wandering Spirit had already hurried down and whispered into the Great Sage’s ear, “Prince Nezha has come to help you.” The Novice looked upward and saw auspicious clouds curling about; there truly was a deity above. He turned back to the little monsters and said, “Now I shall put away the sky.” The little monsters said, “If you’re going to do it, then do it. Why do you keep mumbling and dawdling?” The Novice replied, “I was just summoning my spirit and reciting the spell.” The little monsters opened their eyes wide to see how he would put away the sky. The Novice tossed the imitation gourd into the air. Just think: it had been transformed from a single hair, so how much could it possibly weigh? The wind over the mountaintop caught it and sent it drifting to and fro for fully half an hour before it finally fell. Atop the Southern Gate of Heaven, Prince Nezha unfurled the black banner with a great flapping sound, concealing the sun, moon, and stars alike. Truly, Heaven and Earth seemed dyed in ink, and the whole universe clothed in indigo. The two little monsters exclaimed in alarm, “It was barely noon when we were speaking just now. How has evening fallen already?” The Novice replied, “Once the sky is put away, you can no longer tell the time. Why shouldn’t it seem like evening?” “Then why is it so terribly dark?” The Novice answered, “The sun, moon, and stars have all been put inside. With no light left outside, how could it not be dark?” A little monster called, “Master, where are you speaking from?” The Novice replied, “Am I not right in front of you?” The little monster reached out and felt him, saying, “I can only hear your voice; I cannot see your face at all. Master, what place are we in?” The Novice deceived him again, saying, “Don’t move your feet. We are now on the shore of the Bohai Sea. If you miss your footing and fall in, you won’t reach the bottom for seven or eight days.” The little monsters cried in terror, “Enough, enough! Release the sky. We understand now that this is how you put it away. If you keep this up and we fall into the sea, we’ll never make it home.”

p.src: The splendid Novice, seeing that they now believed it completely, recited another spell to alert the prince. The prince rolled up the banner, and at once the light of the noonday sun reappeared. The little monsters laughed. “Marvelous! Marvelous! If we failed to trade for such a fine treasure, we would truly be unworthy sons of our household.” Clever Devil handed over the gourd, while Quick-witted Bug produced the pure vase, and together they presented both to the Novice. The Novice handed the imitation gourd to the little monsters in exchange. Having exchanged the treasures, he decided to carry the matter through to the end. He plucked a hair from below his navel, breathed immortal breath upon it, and transformed it into a copper coin. He called, “Lads, take this coin and buy a sheet of paper.” The little monsters asked, “What for?” The Novice replied, “I will draw up a written contract with you. You have exchanged your two treasures that can hold people for my one treasure that can hold the sky. I fear that someone may later feel the bargain was unfair and, after many years have passed, regret it and cause trouble. Therefore we should write a document and each keep a copy as proof.” The little monsters said, “There is neither brush nor ink here. How are we to write any document? Let us swear an oath instead.” The Novice asked, “What oath shall we swear?” The little monsters replied, “We have given our two treasures that can hold people in exchange for your one treasure that can hold the sky. If we ever regret the bargain, may pestilence strike us through all four seasons of the year.” The Novice laughed and said, “I shall certainly never regret it. But if I do, may I likewise suffer pestilence through all four seasons, just as you said.”

p.src: After swearing the oath, he sprang upward, flicked his tail, and leaped before the Southern Gate of Heaven, where he thanked Prince Nezha for helping him by waving the banner. The prince returned to the celestial palace to report the completion of his mission and restored the banner to Zhenwu; of this we shall say no more. The Novice remained standing amid the clouds of heaven and watched the little monsters below.
